Real client IPs through the stream hop, with PROXY protocol
PROXY protocol across the stream hop
I left a loose end: my analytics for customer domains had quietly turned into one visitor. The
block forwards raw TCP, so nothing downstream knows who connected — and once the hops moved to sockets, downstream doesn't even get an address. The peer on a unix socket is just "unix".
This post is the fix: PROXY protocol across the same sockets, and what it took to get Caddy and Nginx to speak it.

The stream server terminates nothing. It peeks at the SNI, picks a backend, and copies bytes from one file descriptor to another. It never parses HTTP, so it can't add headers — there's no HTTP to attach anything to. And it can't decrypt to find out either; that's the whole point of the hop.

So Caddy's idea of the remote address is Nginx's connection, and the app's idea is Caddy. Rate limiting, abuse blocking, logs, analytics: they all see one client. The socket swap made it starker — over loopback TCP at least everyone agreed on
; over a unix socket the peer address is a path that tells you nothing.

The stream hop forwards raw TCP, so nothing downstream ever saw the visitor. PROXY protocol fixes that — here's the setup and the traps that come with it.
I moved Nginx's internal hops to Unix sockets
Unix sockets for the internal Nginx hops

It worked fine. It also bugged me, because both of those hops are just processes on the same machine talking to each other over TCP. One of them is Nginx connecting to itself.
So I swapped both for Unix sockets. The main reason is simple: these hops never leave the machine, so they shouldn't be paying for the network stack at all.

flowchart LR
    Client[Client] -->|HTTPS :443| N["Nginx stream (L4)"]
    N -->|unix socket| H["Nginx http · ssl"]
    N -->|"SNI: custom domain · unix socket"| C["Caddy on-demand TLS"]
    H -->|"HTTP · loopback"| App["App"]
    C -->|"HTTP · loopback"| App
N -->|"SNI: custom domain · unix socket"| C["Caddy on-demand TLS"]
Both hops are processes on the same machine talking to each other. Over TCP that means a full handshake, loopback addressing, ephemeral ports, and
cleanup on every connection — the kernel running its whole networking routine for a conversation that never leaves the box.

A Unix socket skips all of it. The kernel moves bytes directly between the two processes, and there's no network stack in the path. You also drop two arbitrary port numbers that someone, probably you in six months, will have to wonder about.

The socket being a file has a side effect I like too: to connect, you need permission on the socket and on the directory it lives in. Everything here is on one machine that I control, so that's not what drove the change — but it costs nothing.
One directory for all of them
I put both sockets in the same directory, so there's one place to check and one permission rule to reason about:

echo 'd /run/app-sockets 0750 caddy www-data -' | sudo tee /etc/tmpfiles.d/app-sockets.conf
sudo systemd-tmpfiles --create
. Check which user your Nginx workers run as (
) and use that as the group if it isn't

You might wonder how Nginx creates a socket in a directory its workers can't write to. It doesn't need the workers for that. The master process runs as root and creates the listening sockets at startup. The workers, running as
, only have to walk into the directory and connect, and the group's read and execute bits cover that.
is tmpfs. The directory and any stale sockets disappear on reboot, and the tmpfiles rule recreates the directory at boot.

Sockets make sense when you control both ends and the connection never needs to leave the machine. For the Nginx-to-Nginx and Nginx-to-Caddy hops, that's true. The app is a separate process with its own lifecycle, and it's also what

Gotcha: ACME challenges and scanner noise
HTTP-01 needs port 80 to reach Caddy for the customer domain, which the
block from Bug 1 handles. If issuance fails, check first that the customer's DNS actually points at your server.
tls-alpn challenge ... no information found to solve challenge for identifier:
in Caddy's logs every few days. Look at the

field: when it's empty, something connected with the ACME ALPN protocol but sent no hostname. Real validations carry the domain, so this is almost certainly a scanner, and Caddy is correctly refusing it.

curl -sI https://timer.customer.com/        # customer-domain path
curl -sI https://app.example.com/           # main-app path
Both should answer over HTTPS with no certificate warnings. To inspect the certificate Caddy actually issued:
echo | openssl s_client -connect timer.customer.com:443 -servername timer.customer.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -dates
That should show Let's Encrypt as the issuer, with dates that make sense.
